items.title: 1.3.1 Solution of Quadratic Equations by Completing the Square

blocks.text: As we learned in previous classes, completing the square is a powerful and systematic method for solving quadratic equations. The technique rewrites a quadratic equation \(ax^{2} + bx + c = 0\) as a perfect square trinomial, which can then be solved by taking the square root of both sides. It is especially valuable when the quadratic does not factor easily: by completing the square we can solve any quadratic equation, even one with irrational or complex roots.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The idea comes from \((z - h)^{2} = z^{2} - 2hz + h^{2}\). If we have \(z^{2} - 2hz\), adding \(h^{2}\) completes the square. The number to add is (half the coefficient of \(z\))\(^{2}\).
Steps:
1. Make the coefficient of \(z^{2}\) equal to 1 (divide by \(a\)).
2. Move the constant term to the right side.
3. Add (half the coefficient of \(z\))\(^{2}\) to both sides.
4. Write the left side as \((z - h)^{2}\) and take the square root with \(\pm\).
5. If the right side is negative, use \(\sqrt{-k} = i\sqrt{k}\): the roots are complex.

blocks.title: Example 10
blocks.problem: Solve the equation \(2z^{2} - 12z + 50 = 0\) by completing square method and hence express it as a product of its linear factors.
steps:
Given: \(2z^{2} - 12z + 50 = 0\).
To find: its roots by completing the square, and then \(2z^{2} - 12z + 50\) as a product of linear factors.
Method: make the coefficient of \(z^{2}\) equal to 1, add (half the coefficient of \(z\))\(^{2}\) to both sides to get a perfect square, take square roots; then use the corollary \(P(z) = a(z - z_{1})(z - z_{2})\).

Step 1: Divide both sides by 2
\[z^{2} - 6z + 25 = 0\]
Why: completing the square is easiest when the coefficient of \(z^{2}\) is 1.

Step 2: Move the constant and rewrite the middle term
\[z^{2} - 2(3)z = -25\]
Why: writing \(-6z\) as \(-2(3)z\) matches the pattern \(z^{2} - 2hz + h^{2} = (z - h)^{2}\) with \(h = 3\).

Step 3: Add \(3^{2}\) on both sides
\[z^{2} - 2(3)z + 3^{2} = -25 + 3^{2}\]
\[(z - 3)^{2} = -16\]
Why: adding the same number to both sides keeps the equation true, and the left side becomes a perfect square.

Step 4: Take the square root
\[z - 3 = \pm\sqrt{-16}\]
\[\sqrt{-16} = \sqrt{16}\sqrt{-1} = 4i\]
\[z = 3 \pm 4i\]
Why: a negative number under the square root gives an imaginary number; \(\pm\) is needed because both \(4i\) and \(-4i\) square to \(-16\).

Step 5: State the roots
\(z = 3 + 4i\) or \(z = 3 - 4i\) are the required complex roots.
Why: a quadratic has exactly two roots in C (Fundamental theorem of algebra).

Step 6: Factorize using the corollary
\[2z^{2} - 12z + 50 = 2(z^{2} - 6z + 25)\]
\[= 2(z - (3 + 4i))(z - (3 - 4i))\]
\[= 2(z - 3 - 4i)(z - 3 + 4i)\]
Why: \(P(z) = a(z - z_{1})(z - z_{2})\) with leading coefficient \(a = 2\) and roots \(3 \pm 4i\). The 2 must stay in front.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Completing the square works for every quadratic, including those with complex roots.
2. Add (half the coefficient of \(z\))\(^{2}\) to both sides after making the \(z^{2}\) coefficient 1.
3. A negative right side gives complex roots \(h \pm i\sqrt{k}\), which are conjugates of each other when the coefficients are real.
4. To factorize, keep the leading coefficient: \(P(z) = a(z - z_{1})(z - z_{2})\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Adding \(h^{2}\) only to the left side.
2. Forgetting the \(\pm\) when taking the square root.
3. Writing \(\sqrt{-16} = -4\): the square root of a negative number is imaginary, \(4i\).
4. Dropping the factor 2 in the final factorization of \(2z^{2} - 12z + 50\).
